meta.title: Who really said "If you believe what you like in the gospels, and reject what you don't like, it is not the gospel you believe, but yourself"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Augustine's idea, modern wording. It paraphrases his Reply to Faustus XVII.3 (trans. 1887): "to believe what you please… is to believe yourselves, and not the gospel."
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'If you believe what you like in the gospels, and reject what you don't like, it is not the gospel you believe, but yourself'?
meta.ogDescription: The thought is genuinely Augustine's (Reply to Faustus XVII.3). The popular wording is a modern paraphrase. It is not a translation of his text.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: The thought is Augustine’s. It closes Reply to Faustus the Manichaean (Contra Faustum), Book XVII, §3, which Richard Stothert translated in 1887 as “For to believe what you please, and not to believe what you please, is to believe yourselves, and not the gospel.” The familiar wording, beginning “If you believe what you like in the gospels…”, is a later paraphrase. No verified translation contains it.

source.excerpt: Your evasions are met on every side. You ought to say plainly that you do not believe the gospel of Christ. For to believe what you please, and not to believe what you please, is to believe yourselves, and not the gospel.
trail: New Advent: Reply to Faustus, Book XVII ↗. Section 3 ends: “For to believe what you please, and not to believe what you please, is to believe yourselves, and not the gospel.” Credited to Richard Stothert, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, First Series, vol. 4 (1887).
CCEL: NPNF vol. 4, Book XVII ↗. A second copy of the same translation, with the same sentence in section 3.

Wikiquote: Augustine of Hippo ↗. Lists the popular wording under “Disputed” and gives George Sweeting’s Who Said That? (1995) as the earliest attribution found. It notes that online sources never say which work the line comes from.
source.excerptNote: Stothert’s 1887 translation, as reproduced on New Advent ↗. Augustine is answering Faustus, who had rejected a saying of Jesus recorded in Matthew (“came not to destroy… but to fulfill” the law and the prophets). Faustus argued that Matthew was not yet a disciple when it was spoken, and that John, who was present, does not record it. The popular quote condenses Augustine’s last sentence and adds “in the gospels” and “reject what you don’t like.”

author.name: Augustine of Hippo
author.heading: About Augustine of Hippo
author.metaLine: 354–430 · Bishop of Hippo Regius, theologian & Church Father
author.bio: Augustine was born at Thagaste in Roman North Africa and died as Bishop of Hippo Regius. He wrote the Confessions and The City of God. As a young man he followed the Manichaeans for years. After his conversion he wrote long polemics against them, including a point-by-point Reply to Faustus the Manichaean.

misattribution.heading: Real idea, rewritten words
misattribution.intro: Most fake Augustine quotes have no source at all. This one does have a real source, but the words people share are not his, nor any verified translation of his. A sharper modern paraphrase has replaced them.

items.why: Augustine tells the Manichaean Faustus that accepting only the parts of the gospel that suit him means trusting himself, not the gospel: “For to believe what you please, and not to believe what you please, is to believe yourselves, and not the gospel” (Stothert trans., 1887 ↗).

“If you believe what you like in the gospels, and reject what you don’t like, it is not the gospel you believe, but yourself” matches no verified translation. Wikiquote ↗ files it under Disputed and gives George Sweeting’s Who Said That? (1995) as the earliest attribution.
Wikiquote notes that online sources “always attribute the quote to Augustine, but never specify in which of his works it is to be found” (Wikiquote ↗). The missing reference is Contra Faustum XVII.3.

misattribution.truthLine: Credit the idea to Augustine, Reply to Faustus the Manichaean XVII.3. When quoting him, use a real translation: “to believe what you please, and not to believe what you please, is to believe yourselves, and not the gospel” (Stothert, 1887 ↗).

context.heading: Why Augustine said it
lead: Faustus was a Manichaean bishop. The Manichaeans accepted parts of the New Testament and rejected others. In Book XVII of Augustine’s reply, Faustus doubts that Jesus ever said he came “not to destroy” the law and the prophets. His reason is that only Matthew records it, and Matthew had not yet been called when it was said. Augustine answers that Faustus readily trusts Mani, who was not there either. He concludes that Faustus “ought to say plainly that you do not believe the gospel of Christ” (New Advent ↗).

So the original line was a rebuke in an argument over scripture, aimed at a particular opponent’s selective canon. The modern paraphrase turns it into a general maxim about cherry-picking scripture. Augustine’s point supports that reading, but the polished wording is not his.
context.pull: To believe what you please, and not to believe what you please, is to believe yourselves, and not the gospel.

sourcesVerified.claim: Reply to Faustus Book XVII §3 ends: 'For to believe what you please, and not to believe what you please, is to believe yourselves, and not the gospel.' Also contains 'You ought to say plainly that you do not believe the gospel of Christ' and 'Your evasions are met on every side.' Translator credit: Richard Stothert, NPNF First Series vol. 4, ed. Philip Schaff (Buffalo, NY: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1887). In section 1, Faustus doubts the 'came not to destroy… but to fulfill' saying because Matthew was not yet chosen and John does not record it.
CCEL NPNF vol. 4 page is Book XVII of the Reply to Faustus, and section 3 contains the same sentence.
Wikiquote lists the popular wording in its Disputed section. Earliest attribution found: George Sweeting, Who Said That? (1995). Online sources always credit Augustine but never say which work.
Augustine was born 13 November 354 at Thagaste, died 28 August 430 at Hippo Regius, and was Bishop of Hippo Regius.
Contra Faustum (Reply to Faustus the Manichaean) is listed with an approximate date of 400; Augustine's chronology is often uncertain.
The Google Books preview page (Sweeting, Who Said That?) visibly displays the quote attributed to Augustine.
